title: Integrating XState with React
description: Connect XState machines to React components using @xstate/react, including useMachine, useSelector, and testing strategies.

blocks.text: XState is framework-agnostic by design, but it ships with first-class React bindings in the @xstate/react package. These bindings handle subscribing to actor state changes, re-rendering components only when relevant state slices change, and cleaning up listeners on unmount. The two primary hooks are useMachine for simple cases and useSelector when you need to select specific pieces of state from a larger machine.

blocks.title: Actor Model in XState v5
blocks.text: XState v5 uses the actor model terminology. A machine becomes an actor when you pass it to createActor. The useMachine hook is syntactic sugar that creates, starts, and stops an actor for you.

data.caption: Data flow from an XState actor into a React component.
data.definition:
flowchart TB
    Machine[XState Machine] --> Actor[createActor]
    Actor --> Service[Running Service]
    Service --> |state changes| Hook[useMachine / useSelector]
    Hook --> |derived state| Component[React Component]
    Component --> |send event| Actor

blocks.text: useMachine is the simplest way to connect a machine to a React component. It returns a tuple containing the current actor snapshot and a send function. When the machine transitions, the component re-renders with the new snapshot. The send function accepts event objects or strings, matching the event types declared in your machine configuration.

blocks.title: useMachine with a Fetch Machine
blocks.content: A practical example connecting a data-fetching machine to a React component.

blocks.text: Prefer state.matches('stateName') over string equality on state.value. matches() is type-safe and works correctly with nested and parallel states.

When a machine is large, you do not want your component to re-render on every state change. useMachine always returns the full snapshot, but you can derive only the data you need using useSelector. The selector function receives the full snapshot and returns a value. React will only re-render when that selected value changes by reference, just like Redux selectors.

blocks.title: useSelector for Granular Updates
blocks.content: Subscribe only to the data you need to avoid unnecessary renders.

blocks.title: When to Use useMachine vs useSelector
items: useMachine: the component renders different UI for every state (loading, error, success).
useSelector: the machine is large, and the component only cares about a small slice of state or context.
useMachine: simpler mental model for small to medium machines.
useSelector: better performance characteristics for high-frequency state updates.

blocks.text: Because XState machines are pure logic, the best tests run against the machine itself, not the React wrapper. Use XState's built-in test utilities to simulate event sequences and assert on the final state and context. React component tests can verify that the correct UI renders for each machine state using testing-library queries.

blocks.title: Testing a Machine Without React
blocks.content: Unit test the machine logic directly with XState's test utilities.

blocks.text: Never test statechart logic inside React component tests alone. If the machine logic is buggy, the component test will still pass because it only verifies the UI. Unit-test the machine first, then write thin component tests to verify rendering.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
points: useMachine is the simplest hook for connecting an XState actor to a React component.
useMachine returns the full snapshot and a send function on every render.
useSelector subscribes to derived slices of actor state to minimize unnecessary re-renders.
Prefer state.matches() over checking state.value directly for type-safe state checks.
Test machines in isolation first using createActor and send, then verify UI rendering separately.
